# =============================================================================
# 03_lmsa.R -- local measures of spatial association on township totals
# Take-home Exercise 2 | ISSS626
#
# Computes, for each of the five armed-conflict variables summed over the whole
# study period, a global Moran's I as the gate, then local Moran's I and
# Getis-Ord Gi* by conditional permutation. A year-by-year local Moran's I of
# all conflict events follows, and then the sensitivity runs that decide how
# much of the cluster map belongs to the data and how much to the analytical
# choices: the neighbour definition, the transformation of the counts, and the
# multiple-testing correction.
# Run from take-home-ex/take-home-ex2/.
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(sf); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(spdep); library(sfdep)
})
source("R/utils.R")

DER  <- "data/derived"
NSIM <- 999
SEED <- 1234

ts      <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "ts_tot.rds"))
nb_an   <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "nb_an.rds"))
nb_knn6 <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "nb_knn6.rds"))
panel_y <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "panel_y.rds"))

VARS <- c(conflict = "All armed-conflict events", battles = "Battles",
          erv = "Explosions / remote violence",
          vac = "Violence against civilians", fatalities = "Reported fatalities")

# ---- Spatial weights -----------------------------------------------------------
# Row standardisation ("W") makes the spatial lag the average of the neighbours,
# which is what the LISA quadrants are read against. Gi* needs the township
# itself inside its own neighbourhood, so a self-inclusive copy is kept for it.
lw_q    <- nb2listw(nb_an,   style = "W")
lw_k    <- nb2listw(nb_knn6, style = "W")
nb_self <- include_self(nb_an)
wt_self <- st_weights(nb_self)

# ---- Global Moran's I: is there spatial structure to localise? ----------------
glob <- lapply(names(VARS), function(v) {
  set.seed(SEED)
  m <- moran.mc(ts[[v]], lw_q, nsim = NSIM, alternative = "greater")
  data.frame(var = v, I = unname(m$statistic), p = m$p.value)
}) |> bind_rows()

# ---- The local statistics -------------------------------------------------------
# Both statistics are tested by conditional permutation: the township's own value
# is held fixed and its neighbours are redrawn from the other 328 townships.
# That avoids the normal approximation, which is a poor reference for counts as
# skewed as these. The p-value carried forward is spdep's two-sided simulated
# p-value ("Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"), not the folded one, which is one-sided and
# would halve every p-value.
local_moran_tbl <- function(x, lw, nsim = NSIM, seed = SEED) {
  set.seed(seed)
  lm <- localmoran_perm(x, lw, nsim = nsim, alternative = "two.sided")
  lag_x <- lag.listw(lw, x)
  tibble(ii = lm[, "Ii"], z_ii = lm[, "Z.Ii"],
         p_ii_sim = lm[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"],
         lag = lag_x,
         quad = lisa_quadrant(x, lag_x, lm[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"]),
         quad_fdr = lisa_quadrant(x, lag_x, lm[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"],
                                  method = "fdr"))
}

local_gi_tbl <- function(x, nb, wt, nsim = NSIM, seed = SEED) {
  set.seed(seed)
  g <- local_gstar_perm(x, nb, wt, nsim = nsim)
  tibble(gi = g$gi_star, p_gi_sim = g$p_sim,
         gi_class = gi_class(g$gi_star, g$p_sim),
         gi_class_fdr = gi_class(g$gi_star, g$p_sim, method = "fdr"))
}

lisa <- lapply(names(VARS), function(v) {
  bind_cols(
    tibble(TS_PCODE = ts$TS_PCODE, var = v, x = ts[[v]]),
    local_moran_tbl(ts[[v]], lw_q),
    local_gi_tbl(ts[[v]], nb_self, wt_self)
  )
}) |> bind_rows()

# ---- Year by year: does the cluster map move? -----------------------------------
# Moran's I is unchanged by rescaling, so the nine-month 2025 needs no per-month
# adjustment here; it would matter only for comparing levels across years.
lisa_year <- lapply(2021:2025, function(y) {
  d <- panel_y |> filter(year == y) |> arrange(TS_PCODE)
  stopifnot(identical(d$TS_PCODE, ts$TS_PCODE))
  bind_cols(tibble(TS_PCODE = d$TS_PCODE, year = y, x = d$conflict),
            local_moran_tbl(d$conflict, lw_q))
}) |> bind_rows()

glob_year <- lapply(2021:2025, function(y) {
  d <- panel_y |> filter(year == y) |> arrange(TS_PCODE)
  set.seed(SEED)
  m <- moran.mc(d$conflict, lw_q, nsim = NSIM, alternative = "greater")
  data.frame(year = y, I = unname(m$statistic), p = m$p.value)
}) |> bind_rows()

# ---- Sensitivity ----------------------------------------------------------------
# Each alternative changes exactly one choice relative to the primary run
# (queen contiguity with the two island links, raw counts, unadjusted p < 0.05)
# and reports how many townships keep the same class. The density variant
# divides by township area, which mainly tests whether the large Shan and
# Kachin townships are hot only because they are large.
sens_spec <- list(
  "Primary (queen, raw counts)"   = list(x = function(d) d$conflict,            lw = lw_q),
  "k = 6 nearest neighbours"      = list(x = function(d) d$conflict,            lw = lw_k),
  "log(1 + count)"                = list(x = function(d) log1p(d$conflict),     lw = lw_q),
  "Events per 1,000 km²"          = list(x = function(d) 1000 * d$conflict / d$area_km2, lw = lw_q)
)

sens <- lapply(names(sens_spec), function(nm) {
  s <- sens_spec[[nm]]
  out <- local_moran_tbl(s$x(ts), s$lw)
  tibble(TS_PCODE = ts$TS_PCODE, spec = nm, quad = out$quad, quad_fdr = out$quad_fdr)
}) |> bind_rows()

prim <- sens |> filter(spec == names(sens_spec)[1]) |> select(TS_PCODE, quad_p = quad)
sens_summary <- sens |>
  left_join(prim, by = "TS_PCODE") |>
  group_by(spec) |>
  summarise(`High-High` = sum(quad == "High-High"), `Low-Low` = sum(quad == "Low-Low"),
            `High-Low` = sum(quad == "High-Low"), `Low-High` = sum(quad == "Low-High"),
            `Survive FDR` = sum(quad_fdr != "Insignificant"),
            `Same class as primary` = sum(quad == quad_p),
            `HH kept` = sum(quad == "High-High" & quad_p == "High-High"),
            .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(spec = factor(spec, levels = names(sens_spec))) |>
  arrange(spec)

# ---- Save -----------------------------------------------------------------------
saveRDS(list(vars = VARS, nsim = NSIM, seed = SEED, glob = glob, lisa = lisa,
             lisa_year = lisa_year, glob_year = glob_year, sens = sens,
             sens_summary = sens_summary),
        file.path(DER, "lmsa.rds"))

cat("\n== Global Moran's I ==\n"); print(glob, digits = 3)
cat("\n== LISA quadrants (p < 0.05) ==\n")
print(lisa |> count(var, quad) |> pivot_wider(names_from = quad, values_from = n, values_fill = 0))
cat("\n== Gi* classes (p < 0.05) ==\n")
print(lisa |> count(var, gi_class) |> pivot_wider(names_from = gi_class, values_from = n, values_fill = 0))
cat("\n== Surviving FDR ==\n")
print(lisa |> group_by(var) |> summarise(lisa_fdr = sum(quad_fdr != "Insignificant"),
                                          gi_fdr = sum(gi_class_fdr != "Insignificant")))
cat("\n== By year ==\n"); print(glob_year, digits = 3)
print(lisa_year |> count(year, quad) |> pivot_wider(names_from = quad, values_from = n, values_fill = 0))

# =============================================================================
# 04_ehsa.R -- space-time cube, Mann-Kendall and emerging hot spot analysis
# Take-home Exercise 2 | ISSS626
#
# Three stages.
#   1. Validation. sfdep::emerging_hotspot_analysis() is run on the quarterly
#      cube of all conflict events and its output is checked against an
#      independent computation of the same statistic (R/ehsa.R). Two defects are
#      measured rather than asserted: the row labels depend on the order of the
#      geometry, and the permutation null pools every period of the cube.
#   2. Primary analysis. For each of the five conflict variables, space-time
#      Gi* with one quarter of temporal lag, a period-conditional permutation
#      null, the Mann-Kendall test on each township's Gi* series, and sfdep's
#      own classification rules at p = 0.05.
#   3. Sensitivity. The time lag, the neighbour definition, the time unit, and
#      the p-value convention are each changed in turn.
# Run from take-home-ex/take-home-ex2/.
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(sf); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(spdep); library(sfdep)
})
source("R/utils.R")
source("R/ehsa.R")

DER  <- "data/derived"
SEED <- 1234
NSIM <- 999          # period-conditional permutations, primary analysis
NSIM_SFDEP <- 199    # sfdep's own default, used for the validation run
ALPHA <- 0.05

ts_an   <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "township_an.rds"))
ts_raw  <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "township.rds"))
nb_an   <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "nb_an.rds"))
nb_knn6 <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "nb_knn6.rds"))
panel_q <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "panel_q.rds"))
panel_m <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "panel_m.rds"))

VARS <- c(conflict = "All armed-conflict events", battles = "Battles",
          erv = "Explosions / remote violence",
          vac = "Violence against civilians", fatalities = "Reported fatalities")

locs <- ts_an$TS_PCODE
stopifnot(!is.unsorted(locs))     # the order sfdep's labels silently assume
nb_self <- include_self(nb_an)

# ---- The space-time cube --------------------------------------------------------
# sfdep's spacetime object binds the panel to the geometry and is checked for
# completeness: every township in every quarter, exactly once.
geo <- ts_an |> select(TS_PCODE)
geo$nb <- nb_self                    # assigned directly: dplyr >= 1.2 refuses
geo$wt <- st_weights(nb_self)        # an `nb` object inside mutate()

cube_q <- spacetime(as.data.frame(panel_q), geo,
                    .loc_col = "TS_PCODE", .time_col = "period")
stopifnot(is_spacetime_cube(cube_q))

cube_info <- list(n_locs = length(locs), n_times = length(unique(panel_q$period)),
                  n_bins = nrow(panel_q),
                  periods = sort(unique(panel_q$period)))

# ---- 1. Validation against sfdep --------------------------------------------------
X_conf <- panel_matrix(panel_q, "conflict", locs)
G_conf <- gi_spt(X_conf, nb_self, k = 1L)
mk_conf <- apply(G_conf, 1, function(g) Kendall::MannKendall(g)$tau)

ehsa_sf <- cache_rds("ehsa_sfdep_conflict", {
  set.seed(SEED)
  emerging_hotspot_analysis(cube_q, "conflict", k = 1, include_gi = TRUE,
                            nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt",
                            nsim = NSIM_SFDEP, threshold = ALPHA)
})
gi_sf <- attr(ehsa_sf, "gi_star")
gi_sf$TS_PCODE <- rep(locs, times = cube_info$n_times)
gi_sf$period   <- rep(cube_info$periods, each = length(locs))

val <- list()
# (a) The deterministic part, Gi* itself, is the same statistic.
val$max_gi_diff <- max(abs(as.vector(G_conf) - gi_sf$gi_star))
# (b) With the geometry sorted by location id, sfdep's tau is the township's own.
tau_sorted <- data.frame(location = ehsa_sf$location, tau_sf = ehsa_sf$tau) |>
  left_join(data.frame(location = locs, tau_me = mk_conf), by = "location")
val$max_tau_diff_sorted <- max(abs(tau_sorted$tau_sf - tau_sorted$tau_me))

# (c) The same cube with the geometry in MIMU's delivered order. Only tau is
# compared, and tau does not depend on the permutations, so a handful of them
# is enough here.
ord <- match(ts_raw$TS_PCODE[ts_raw$TS_PCODE %in% locs], locs)
inv <- integer(length(locs)); inv[ord] <- seq_along(ord)
nb_mimu <- lapply(seq_along(ord), function(p) sort(inv[nb_an[[ord[p]]]]))
class(nb_mimu) <- "nb"; attr(nb_mimu, "region.id") <- locs[ord]
nb_mimu <- include_self(nb_mimu)
geo_mimu <- ts_an[ord, ] |> select(TS_PCODE)
geo_mimu$nb <- nb_mimu
geo_mimu$wt <- st_weights(nb_mimu)
cube_mimu <- spacetime(as.data.frame(panel_q), geo_mimu,
                       .loc_col = "TS_PCODE", .time_col = "period")

ehsa_mimu <- cache_rds("ehsa_sfdep_conflict_mimu_order", {
  set.seed(SEED)
  emerging_hotspot_analysis(cube_mimu, "conflict", k = 1,
                            nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt",
                            nsim = 19, threshold = ALPHA)
})
tau_mimu <- data.frame(location = ehsa_mimu$location, tau_sf = ehsa_mimu$tau) |>
  left_join(data.frame(location = locs, tau_me = mk_conf), by = "location")
val$share_wrong_mimu  <- mean(abs(tau_mimu$tau_sf - tau_mimu$tau_me) > 1e-9)
val$cor_tau_mimu      <- cor(tau_mimu$tau_sf, tau_mimu$tau_me)
# Relabelling sfdep's rows in alphabetical order of location recovers the
# right answer exactly, which pins the cause on the labelling step.
tau_relab <- data.frame(location = sort(ehsa_mimu$location), tau_sf = ehsa_mimu$tau) |>
  left_join(data.frame(location = locs, tau_me = mk_conf), by = "location")
val$max_tau_diff_relabelled <- max(abs(tau_relab$tau_sf - tau_relab$tau_me))
val$class_changed_mimu <- sum(
  ehsa_mimu$classification[match(locs, ehsa_mimu$location)] !=
  ehsa_sf$classification[match(locs, ehsa_sf$location)])
val$tau_mimu <- tau_mimu

# (d) Feeding sfdep's own per-bin p-values through ehsa_classify() with sfdep's
# rules unchanged reproduces sfdep's classification exactly, so the classifier
# is not a source of difference either.
P_sf <- matrix(gi_sf$p_sim, nrow = length(locs))
cls_sf_check <- ehsa_classify(G_conf, P_sf, ALPHA, locs, corrected = FALSE)
val$classifier_identical <- identical(
  cls_sf_check$classification,
  sub("oscilating", "oscillating", ehsa_sf$classification[match(locs, ehsa_sf$location)]))

# ---- 2. Primary analysis: period-conditional null --------------------------------
# Only the expensive part, Gi* and its permutation p-values, is cached. The
# classification is cheap and is always recomputed, so a change to the class
# rules can never be hidden behind a stale cache.
run_ehsa <- function(panel, var, nb_s, k = 1L, nsim = NSIM, seed = SEED) {
  X <- panel_matrix(panel, var, locs)
  G <- gi_spt(X, nb_s, k = k)
  P <- gi_spt_perm(X, nb_s, k = k, nsim = nsim, seed = seed)
  list(X = X, G = G, p_fold = P$p_fold, p_two = P$p_two)
}
add_classes <- function(r) {
  r$cls      <- ehsa_classify(r$G, r$p_fold, ALPHA, locs)
  r$cls_two  <- ehsa_classify(r$G, r$p_two,  ALPHA, locs)
  r$cls_sfdep_rules <- ehsa_classify(r$G, r$p_fold, ALPHA, locs, corrected = FALSE)
  r
}

ehsa <- lapply(names(VARS), function(v) {
  add_classes(cache_rds(paste0("ehsa_pc_q_k1_", v), run_ehsa(panel_q, v, nb_self)))
}) |> setNames(names(VARS))

# Townships whose class changes when the one sfdep rule is corrected.
rule_fix <- lapply(names(VARS), function(v) {
  r <- ehsa[[v]]
  ch <- which(r$cls$classification != r$cls_sfdep_rules$classification)
  tibble(var = v, TS_PCODE = locs[ch],
         sfdep_rule = r$cls_sfdep_rules$classification[ch],
         corrected  = r$cls$classification[ch],
         n_hot  = rowSums(r$p_fold[ch, , drop = FALSE] <= ALPHA & r$G[ch, , drop = FALSE] > 0),
         n_cold = rowSums(r$p_fold[ch, , drop = FALSE] <= ALPHA & r$G[ch, , drop = FALSE] < 0))
}) |> bind_rows()

# Per-quarter counts of significant hot and cold bins under the two nulls: the
# figure that shows where sfdep's classes come from.
bins_by_null <- bind_rows(
  gi_sf |> group_by(period) |>
    summarise(hot = sum(p_sim <= ALPHA & gi_star > 0),
              cold = sum(p_sim <= ALPHA & gi_star < 0), .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(null = "sfdep: pooled over all quarters"),
  tibble(period = rep(cube_info$periods, each = length(locs)),
         g = as.vector(ehsa$conflict$G), p = as.vector(ehsa$conflict$p_fold)) |>
    group_by(period) |>
    summarise(hot = sum(p <= ALPHA & g > 0), cold = sum(p <= ALPHA & g < 0),
              .groups = "drop") |>
    mutate(null = "Period-conditional")
) |>
  left_join(panel_q |> group_by(period) |> summarise(national = sum(conflict)),
            by = "period")

# The two classifications side by side, for all conflict events.
cls_compare <- tibble(
  TS_PCODE = locs,
  sfdep = ehsa_label(sub("oscilating", "oscillating",
                         ehsa_sf$classification[match(locs, ehsa_sf$location)])),
  pc    = ehsa_label(ehsa$conflict$cls$classification)
)

# sfdep's EHSA for the other four variables, so that the comparison of class
# counts covers every variable and not only the one examined in detail.
ehsa_sf_all <- lapply(names(VARS), function(v) {
  e <- if (v == "conflict") ehsa_sf else cache_rds(paste0("ehsa_sfdep_", v), {
    set.seed(SEED)
    emerging_hotspot_analysis(cube_q, v, k = 1, nb_col = "nb", wt_col = "wt",
                              nsim = NSIM_SFDEP, threshold = ALPHA)
  })
  tibble(var = v, TS_PCODE = e$location,
         classification = ehsa_label(sub("oscilating", "oscillating", e$classification)))
}) |> bind_rows()

# ---- How many townships would each class hold by chance? ---------------------------
# Every township is tested once per quarter, 19 times, and a single significant
# hot quarter with no significant cold one is enough for "sporadic hot spot".
# The class counts therefore need a reference. Here each township's complete
# 19-quarter history is moved to a randomly chosen location, which keeps every
# series and its serial dependence intact and destroys only the spatial
# arrangement, and the whole EHSA is re-run. The p-values inside each null cube
# use 99 permutations, which resolves the 0.05 threshold.
# Each null cube also records how many quarters every township spends as a
# significant hot spot, so that the count of significant quarters, which says
# more than the class label does, gets a reference distribution of its own.
NNULL <- 99
class_levels <- names(PAL_EHSA)
null_sim <- cache_rds("ehsa_null_conflict_v3", {
  set.seed(SEED)
  seeds <- sample.int(1e6, NNULL)
  lapply(seq_len(NNULL), function(r) {
    set.seed(seeds[r])
    Xn <- X_conf[sample.int(nrow(X_conf)), , drop = FALSE]
    Gn <- gi_spt(Xn, nb_self, k = 1L)
    Pn <- gi_spt_perm(Xn, nb_self, k = 1L, nsim = 99, seed = seeds[r])
    list(classes = as.vector(table(factor(
           ehsa_label(ehsa_classify(Gn, Pn$p_fold, ALPHA, locs)$classification),
           levels = class_levels))),
         n_hot  = tabulate(rowSums(Pn$p_fold <= ALPHA & Gn > 0) + 1L, nbins = ncol(Xn) + 1L),
         n_cold = tabulate(rowSums(Pn$p_fold <= ALPHA & Gn < 0) + 1L, nbins = ncol(Xn) + 1L))
  })
})
null_counts <- sapply(null_sim, `[[`, "classes")
rownames(null_counts) <- class_levels
# Pooled over all null cubes: the distribution of significant hot (and cold)
# quarters for a township whose neighbours are a random set.
null_nq <- tibble(
  k      = 0:cube_info$n_times,
  p_hot  = rowSums(sapply(null_sim, `[[`, "n_hot"))  / (NNULL * length(locs)),
  p_cold = rowSums(sapply(null_sim, `[[`, "n_cold")) / (NNULL * length(locs))
) |>
  mutate(surv_hot = rev(cumsum(rev(p_hot))), surv_cold = rev(cumsum(rev(p_cold))))

obs_counts <- as.vector(table(factor(ehsa_label(ehsa$conflict$cls$classification),
                                     levels = class_levels)))
null_tbl <- tibble(
  class    = factor(class_levels, levels = class_levels),
  observed = obs_counts,
  null_mean = rowMeans(null_counts),
  null_lo  = apply(null_counts, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  null_hi  = apply(null_counts, 1, quantile, 0.975),
  p_upper  = (rowSums(null_counts >= obs_counts) + 1) / (NNULL + 1)
) |>
  filter(observed > 0 | null_mean > 0.5)

# ---- 3. Sensitivity (all conflict events) ------------------------------------------
# One choice changes at a time; the time-lag variants and the neighbour variant
# use the quarterly cube, and the monthly variant keeps k = 1, i.e. one month.
nb_knn6_self <- include_self(nb_knn6)

sens_runs <- list(
  "k = 0 (no time lag)"  = cache_rds("ehsa_pc_q_k0_conflict", run_ehsa(panel_q, "conflict", nb_self, k = 0L)),
  "k = 2 (two quarters)" = cache_rds("ehsa_pc_q_k2_conflict", run_ehsa(panel_q, "conflict", nb_self, k = 2L)),
  "k = 6 nearest neighbours" = cache_rds("ehsa_pc_q_knn6_conflict", run_ehsa(panel_q, "conflict", nb_knn6_self)),
  "Monthly cube (57 months)" = cache_rds("ehsa_pc_m_k1_conflict", run_ehsa(panel_m, "conflict", nb_self))
) |> lapply(add_classes)

prim_cls <- ehsa_label(ehsa$conflict$cls$classification)
sens_tbl <- bind_rows(
  tibble(spec = "Primary (quarterly, k = 1, queen, folded p)", cls = prim_cls),
  tibble(spec = "Two-sided p ≤ 0.05", cls = ehsa_label(ehsa$conflict$cls_two$classification)),
  lapply(names(sens_runs), function(nm)
    tibble(spec = nm, cls = ehsa_label(sens_runs[[nm]]$cls$classification))) |> bind_rows()
) |>
  group_by(spec) |>
  mutate(same = cls == prim_cls) |>
  summarise(
    `Hot classes`  = sum(grepl("hot spot", cls)),
    `Cold classes` = sum(grepl("cold spot", cls)),
    `No pattern`   = sum(cls == "No pattern detected"),
    `Same class as primary` = sum(same),
    `Hot/cold side kept` = sum(sub(".* (hot|cold) spot$", "\\1", cls) ==
                               sub(".* (hot|cold) spot$", "\\1", prim_cls)),
    .groups = "drop")

# Serial dependence in the Gi* series. The Mann-Kendall test assumes independent
# observations; with k = 1 consecutive bins share a quarter of data, which
# induces positive autocorrelation and makes the trend test too liberal.
acf1 <- function(G) apply(G, 1, function(g) {
  if (sd(g) == 0) return(NA_real_)
  stats::acf(g, lag.max = 1, plot = FALSE)$acf[2]
})
serial <- tibble(
  spec = c("k = 1", "k = 0"),
  median_acf1 = c(median(acf1(ehsa$conflict$G), na.rm = TRUE),
                  median(acf1(sens_runs[["k = 0 (no time lag)"]]$G), na.rm = TRUE)),
  share_sig_mk = c(mean(ehsa$conflict$cls$p_value < ALPHA),
                   mean(sens_runs[["k = 0 (no time lag)"]]$cls$p_value < ALPHA))
)

# ---- Save ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
slim <- function(r) r[c("G", "p_fold", "p_two", "cls", "cls_two")]
saveRDS(list(
  vars = VARS, alpha = ALPHA, nsim = NSIM, nsim_sfdep = NSIM_SFDEP, seed = SEED,
  locs = locs, cube_info = cube_info,
  validation = val, bins_by_null = bins_by_null, cls_compare = cls_compare,
  null_classes = null_tbl, null_counts = null_counts, nnull = NNULL,
  rule_fix = rule_fix,
  null_nq = null_nq,
  sfdep_all = ehsa_sf_all,
  results = lapply(ehsa, slim),
  sens = sens_tbl, sens_monthly = slim(sens_runs[["Monthly cube (57 months)"]]),
  sens_k0 = slim(sens_runs[["k = 0 (no time lag)"]]),
  serial = serial
), file.path(DER, "ehsa.rds"))

cat("\n== Validation ==\n"); str(val[setdiff(names(val), "tau_mimu")])
cat("\n== Significant bins per quarter, by null ==\n")
print(bins_by_null |> pivot_wider(id_cols = c(period, national), names_from = null,
                                  values_from = c(hot, cold)), n = 30)
cat("\n== Classes, primary ==\n")
for (v in names(VARS)) { cat("--", v, "\n"); print(table(ehsa_label(ehsa[[v]]$cls$classification))[table(ehsa_label(ehsa[[v]]$cls$classification)) > 0]) }
cat("\n== sfdep vs period-conditional (conflict) ==\n")
print(table(sfdep = cls_compare$sfdep, pc = cls_compare$pc) |> as.data.frame() |> filter(Freq > 0) |> arrange(desc(Freq)))
cat("\n== Corrected intensifying-hot-spot rule: classes changed ==\n"); print(rule_fix)
cat("\n== Class counts against spatial randomness ==\n"); print(null_tbl, width = 120)
cat("\n== Significant quarters under the null (survival) ==\n"); print(null_nq, n = 25)
cat("\n== Sensitivity ==\n"); print(sens_tbl, width = 160)
cat("\n== Serial dependence ==\n"); print(serial)

# =============================================================================
# 05_markov.R -- value-added analysis: does armed conflict spread to neighbours?
# Take-home Exercise 2 | ISSS626
#
# EHSA classifies each township by the history of its own Gi* series. It does
# not ask whether a township's next quarter depends on what its neighbours are
# doing now, which is the question a diffusion argument turns on. This script
# answers it in three ways that rest on different assumptions:
#   A. a spatial Markov chain (Rey 2001): quarterly transition matrices between
#      four conflict-intensity states, conditioned on the state of the
#      neighbourhood, tested for homogeneity by likelihood ratio and by a
#      permutation null that keeps every township's own history intact;
#   B. a fixed-effects logit of escalation, which asks whether the neighbourhood
#      effect survives once each township's permanent propensity and each
#      quarter's nationwide shock are removed;
#   C. the timing of each township's first entry into sustained conflict,
#      tested against random reassignment of the same onset dates.
# Run from take-home-ex/take-home-ex2/.
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(sf); library(dplyr); library(tidyr); library(spdep)
  library(sandwich); library(lmtest)
})
source("R/utils.R")
source("R/ehsa.R")      # panel_matrix()

DER  <- "data/derived"
SEED <- 1234
NPERM <- 999

ts_an   <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "township_an.rds"))
nb_an   <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "nb_an.rds"))
panel_q <- readRDS(file.path(DER, "panel_q.rds"))

locs    <- ts_an$TS_PCODE
periods <- sort(unique(panel_q$period))
lw      <- nb2listw(nb_an, style = "W")

# ---- States ----------------------------------------------------------------------
# Four states on events per quarter. The cut points are round numbers that fall
# close to the quartiles of the pooled township-quarter distribution, and they
# read as an operational scale: none; sporadic (1-3, about one a month or
# less); sustained (4-14, up to about one a week); intense (15 or more).
BRK    <- c(-Inf, 0.5, 3.5, 14.5, Inf)
STATES <- c("None", "Sporadic", "Sustained", "Intense")
to_state <- function(x) factor(cut(x, BRK, labels = STATES), levels = STATES)

X <- panel_matrix(panel_q, "conflict", locs)          # 329 x 19
L <- apply(X, 2, function(x) lag.listw(lw, x))        # neighbourhood mean
S  <- matrix(as.integer(to_state(X)), nrow(X))
SL <- matrix(as.integer(to_state(L)), nrow(X))

TT <- ncol(X)
trans <- tibble(
  TS_PCODE = rep(locs, times = TT - 1),
  t        = rep(seq_len(TT - 1), each = nrow(X)),
  from     = as.vector(S[, -TT]),
  to       = as.vector(S[, -1]),
  lag      = as.vector(SL[, -TT]),
  own_n    = as.vector(X[, -TT]),
  lag_n    = as.vector(L[, -TT])
)

# ---- A. Spatial Markov chain -----------------------------------------------------
k <- length(STATES)
count_mat <- function(from, to) {
  table(factor(from, levels = seq_len(k)), factor(to, levels = seq_len(k)))
}
row_prob <- function(m) { r <- rowSums(m); sweep(m, 1, ifelse(r == 0, 1, r), "/") }

N_pool <- count_mat(trans$from, trans$to)
P_pool <- row_prob(N_pool)
N_cond <- lapply(seq_len(k), function(l) count_mat(trans$from[trans$lag == l], trans$to[trans$lag == l]))
P_cond <- lapply(N_cond, row_prob)

# Likelihood-ratio test that the conditional matrices equal the pooled one
# (Bickenbach and Bode 2003). Degrees of freedom count only the cells that can
# vary: for each origin state, (non-empty destination cells - 1) times
# (neighbourhood classes in which that origin occurs - 1).
lr_homog <- function(lag_state) {
  Np <- count_mat(trans$from, trans$to); Pp <- row_prob(Np)
  Q <- 0
  for (l in seq_len(k)) {
    sel <- lag_state == l
    if (!any(sel)) next
    Nl <- count_mat(trans$from[sel], trans$to[sel]); Pl <- row_prob(Nl)
    pos <- Nl > 0
    Q <- Q + 2 * sum(Nl[pos] * log(Pl[pos] / Pp[pos]))
  }
  Q
}
Q_obs <- lr_homog(trans$lag)
b_i <- rowSums(N_pool > 0)
c_i <- vapply(seq_len(k), function(i) sum(vapply(N_cond, function(m) sum(m[i, ]) > 0, logical(1))), numeric(1))
df_Q <- sum((b_i - 1) * (c_i - 1))
p_Q  <- pchisq(Q_obs, df_Q, lower.tail = FALSE)

# The chi-square reference assumes independent transitions, and these are
# neither independent over time nor over space. The permutation null keeps each
# township's own sequence of states and each neighbourhood's sequence of
# states, and breaks only the pairing between them: township i is given the
# neighbourhood history of a randomly chosen township. Nationwide swings stay
# in both halves, so they cannot produce a difference on their own.
onset_contrast <- function(lag_state) {
  q <- trans$from == 1
  mean(trans$to[q & lag_state >= 3] > 1) - mean(trans$to[q & lag_state == 1] > 1)
}
C_obs <- onset_contrast(trans$lag)

set.seed(SEED)
perm <- replicate(NPERM, {
  pi_ <- sample.int(nrow(X))
  lag_p <- as.vector(SL[pi_, -TT])
  c(Q = lr_homog(lag_p), C = onset_contrast(lag_p))
})
p_Q_perm <- (sum(perm["Q", ] >= Q_obs) + 1) / (NPERM + 1)
p_C_perm <- (sum(perm["C", ] >= C_obs) + 1) / (NPERM + 1)

# Expected quarters a quiet township stays quiet, by neighbourhood, if the
# neighbourhood did not change: the mean of a geometric waiting time.
stay_quiet <- vapply(P_cond, function(P) P[1, 1], numeric(1))
wait_q <- 1 / (1 - stay_quiet)

markov <- list(
  states = STATES, breaks = BRK, n_trans = nrow(trans),
  N_pool = N_pool, P_pool = P_pool, N_cond = N_cond, P_cond = P_cond,
  Q = Q_obs, df = df_Q, p_chisq = p_Q,
  perm_Q = perm["Q", ], perm_C = perm["C", ], p_Q_perm = p_Q_perm,
  C_obs = C_obs, p_C_perm = p_C_perm,
  stay_quiet = stay_quiet, wait_quarters = wait_q,
  state_share = prop.table(table(factor(S, levels = seq_len(k))))
)

# ---- B. Fixed-effects logit of escalation ---------------------------------------
# Outcome: the township moves to a higher state next quarter. Only township-
# quarters that can escalate (not already Intense) enter. Township fixed effects
# absorb any permanent difference between townships, which is the alternative
# explanation for the Markov result: violent regions are violent everywhere,
# so a township with violent neighbours would escalate more often even with no
# spillover at all. Quarter fixed effects absorb nationwide shocks. What is left
# for the neighbourhood term is whether a township escalates more in the
# quarters after its own neighbourhood has been more violent than usual.
esc <- trans |>
  filter(from < k) |>
  mutate(escalate = as.integer(to > from),
         lag_log  = log1p(lag_n),
         from_f   = factor(STATES[from], levels = STATES[-k]),
         TS_f = factor(TS_PCODE), t_f = factor(t))

fit_pooled <- glm(escalate ~ lag_log + from_f, data = esc, family = binomial)
fit_tfe    <- glm(escalate ~ lag_log + from_f + t_f, data = esc, family = binomial)
fit_fe     <- glm(escalate ~ lag_log + from_f + t_f + TS_f, data = esc, family = binomial)

coef_row <- function(fit, label) {
  ct <- coeftest(fit, vcov. = vcovCL(fit, cluster = ~ TS_PCODE, type = "HC0"))
  b  <- ct["lag_log", "Estimate"]; se <- ct["lag_log", "Std. Error"]
  tibble(model = label, beta = b, se = se,
         OR = exp(b), lo = exp(b - 1.96 * se), hi = exp(b + 1.96 * se),
         p = ct["lag_log", "Pr(>|z|)"], n = nobs(fit))
}
fe_tbl <- bind_rows(
  coef_row(fit_pooled, "No fixed effects"),
  coef_row(fit_tfe,    "Quarter fixed effects"),
  coef_row(fit_fe,     "Township and quarter fixed effects")
)

# The neighbourhood effect stated on the probability scale, for a quiet
# township, from the full fixed-effects model: neighbourhood mean of 0 against
# 15 events in the quarter, averaging the prediction over every quiet
# township-quarter in the data.
quiet <- esc |> filter(from_f == "None")
pr_at <- function(v) mean(predict(fit_fe, newdata = mutate(quiet, lag_log = log1p(v)), type = "response"))
fe_effect <- tibble(neigh_mean = c(0, 1, 4, 15),
                    p_escalate = vapply(c(0, 1, 4, 15), pr_at, numeric(1)))

# ---- C. Onset of sustained conflict ----------------------------------------------
# Onset: the first quarter in which a township records 4 or more events.
# Townships already at that level in 2021 Q1 are left out of the test, since
# their onset precedes the window. An onset is "adjacent" if at least one queen
# neighbour reached sustained conflict in an EARLIER quarter, which is the
# footprint expansion diffusion leaves; otherwise it is a jump.
SUST <- 4
first_q <- apply(X >= SUST, 1, function(r) if (any(r)) which(r)[1] else NA_integer_)

adjacent_share <- function(onset) {
  idx <- which(!is.na(onset) & onset > 1)
  adj <- vapply(idx, function(i) {
    o <- onset[nb_an[[i]]]
    any(!is.na(o) & o < onset[i])
  }, logical(1))
  list(share = mean(adj), adj = adj, idx = idx)
}
on_obs <- adjacent_share(first_q)

# Null: the same onset dates, dealt at random among the townships that had an
# onset inside the window. Townships active from the start and townships that
# never reached sustained conflict keep their status, so the null preserves how
# many townships were already burning and where.
movable <- which(!is.na(first_q) & first_q > 1)
set.seed(SEED)
on_null <- replicate(NPERM, {
  o <- first_q
  o[movable] <- sample(o[movable])
  adjacent_share(o)$share
})
p_onset <- (sum(on_null >= on_obs$share) + 1) / (NPERM + 1)

onset_tbl <- tibble(
  TS_PCODE = locs,
  onset_t  = first_q,
  onset    = periods[first_q],
  type = case_when(
    is.na(first_q) ~ "Never sustained",
    first_q == 1   ~ "Sustained from 2021 Q1",
    TRUE           ~ NA_character_)
)
onset_tbl$type[on_obs$idx] <- ifelse(on_obs$adj, "Adjacent onset", "Jump onset")

onset <- list(threshold = SUST, share_obs = on_obs$share,
              null = on_null, p = p_onset, n_onsets = length(movable),
              table = onset_tbl)

# ---- D. Does knowing the neighbourhood help to anticipate escalation? -----------
# A back-test. The transition matrices are estimated only on transitions that
# begin before 2024 Q4, and then used to predict whether each township that was
# not yet in sustained conflict reaches sustained or intense conflict in the
# following quarter, for the three transitions that begin in 2024 Q4, 2025 Q1
# and 2025 Q2. Two predictors are compared: the township's own state alone
# (pooled matrix), and its own state together with its neighbourhood's state
# (conditional matrices). AUC is computed as the Mann-Whitney probability that
# a township that did escalate was given a higher score than one that did not.
cut_t <- which(periods == as.Date("2024-10-01"))
train <- trans |> filter(t < cut_t)
test  <- trans |> filter(t >= cut_t, from <= 2)

P_pool_tr <- row_prob(count_mat(train$from, train$to))
P_cond_tr <- lapply(seq_len(k), function(l)
  row_prob(count_mat(train$from[train$lag == l], train$to[train$lag == l])))

test <- test |>
  mutate(y = as.integer(to >= 3),
         p_own = P_pool_tr[cbind(from, 3)] + P_pool_tr[cbind(from, 4)],
         p_nb  = vapply(seq_len(n()), function(r) {
           P <- P_cond_tr[[lag[r]]]; P[from[r], 3] + P[from[r], 4]
         }, numeric(1)))

auc <- function(score, y) {
  r <- rank(score); n1 <- sum(y == 1); n0 <- sum(y == 0)
  (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
}
backtest <- tibble(
  predictor = c("Own state only", "Own state + neighbourhood state"),
  auc   = c(auc(test$p_own, test$y), auc(test$p_nb, test$y)),
  brier = c(mean((test$p_own - test$y)^2), mean((test$p_nb - test$y)^2)),
  n = nrow(test), events = sum(test$y)
)

# Forward look: every township's probability of being in sustained or intense
# conflict in 2025 Q4, from its own state and its neighbourhood's state in
# 2025 Q3, using the matrices estimated on the whole period.
last <- TT
outlook <- tibble(
  TS_PCODE = locs,
  own   = S[, last], lag = SL[, last],
  own_n = X[, last], lag_n = L[, last]
) |>
  mutate(p_next = vapply(seq_len(n()), function(r) {
    P <- P_cond[[lag[r]]]; P[own[r], 3] + P[own[r], 4]
  }, numeric(1)),
  own_state = STATES[own], lag_state = STATES[lag])

# ---- Save -------------------------------------------------------------------------
saveRDS(list(markov = markov, fe = fe_tbl, fe_effect = fe_effect,
             onset = onset, backtest = backtest, outlook = outlook,
             nperm = NPERM, seed = SEED),
        file.path(DER, "markov.rds"))

cat("\n== Pooled transition matrix ==\n"); print(round(P_pool, 3))
for (l in seq_len(k)) { cat("\n-- neighbourhood:", STATES[l], " (n =", sum(N_cond[[l]]), ")\n"); print(round(P_cond[[l]], 3)) }
cat(sprintf("\nLR homogeneity Q = %.1f, df = %d, chi-sq p = %.3g, permutation p = %.3f\n", Q_obs, df_Q, p_Q, p_Q_perm))
cat(sprintf("onset contrast (sustained/intense vs quiet neighbourhood) = %.3f, permutation p = %.3f (null mean %.3f)\n",
            C_obs, p_C_perm, mean(perm["C", ])))
cat("\nquarters a quiet township stays quiet:\n"); print(setNames(round(wait_q, 2), STATES))
cat("\n== Fixed-effects logit ==\n"); print(fe_tbl, width = 120)
print(fe_effect)
cat(sprintf("\n== Onsets == n = %d, adjacent share = %.3f, null mean = %.3f, p = %.3f\n",
            length(movable), on_obs$share, mean(on_null), p_onset))
print(table(onset_tbl$type))
cat("\n== Back-test ==\n"); print(backtest)
cat("\n== Outlook for 2025 Q4: quiet or sporadic townships with the highest probability ==\n")
print(outlook |> filter(own <= 2) |> arrange(desc(p_next)) |> head(15))

# =============================================================================
# R/ehsa.R -- emerging hot spot analysis with a period-conditional null
# Take-home Exercise 2 | ISSS626
#
# The space-time Gi* below is the statistic sfdep::emerging_hotspot_analysis()
# computes, written out so that it can be checked against sfdep value for value
# (scripts/04_ehsa.R does the check) and so that the one part that is changed
# is visible. That part is the permutation null.
#
# sfdep draws the pseudo-neighbours of a bin from every bin in the cube, at any
# location and in any period, and replaces the bin's own value as well. When
# the national level of the variable trends, as conflict in Myanmar does, the
# draws for an early, quiet quarter come mostly from later, busier quarters, so
# almost every township looks unusually low; in the busiest quarters the reverse
# happens. The significance of a bin then tracks the national trend rather than
# the township's standing among its contemporaries.
#
# Here the township's own values are held fixed and its neighbours are replaced
# by a random set of other townships, read in the same periods as the real
# neighbours. Each bin is therefore judged only against the other townships of
# its own quarter, which is the comparison the Gi* standardisation already makes.
# =============================================================================

# Observed space-time Gi*.
#   X       n_locs x n_times matrix, rows in the order of `nb_self`
#   nb_self self-inclusive neighbour list (spdep / sfdep `nb`)
#   k       number of earlier periods pooled into each bin's neighbourhood
# Weights are row-standardised within each period copy, as in sfdep, so a bin
# with k earlier periods available has total weight k + 1.
gi_spt <- function(X, nb_self, k = 1L) {
  n  <- nrow(X); TT <- ncol(X)
  w0 <- 1 / lengths(nb_self)
  G  <- matrix(NA_real_, n, TT)
  for (t in seq_len(TT)) {
    sl  <- max(1L, t - k):t
    S   <- rowSums(X[, sl, drop = FALSE])
    lx  <- w0 * vapply(nb_self, function(j) sum(S[j]), numeric(1))
    m   <- length(sl)
    x   <- X[, t]
    Wi  <- m
    S1i <- m * w0
    si2 <- sum((x - mean(x))^2) / n
    VG  <- si2 * ((n * S1i - Wi^2) / (n - 1))
    G[, t] <- (lx - Wi * mean(x)) / sqrt(VG)
  }
  G
}

# Period-conditional permutation p-values for the same statistic. Because the
# expectation and variance of Gi* depend only on the weights and on the
# period's own mean and variance, ranking the neighbourhood sum is equivalent
# to ranking Gi* itself, and is cheaper.
# Returns both the folded p-value that sfdep thresholds (min of the two tails)
# and the two-sided p-value, which is twice it.
gi_spt_perm <- function(X, nb_self, k = 1L, nsim = 499L, seed = 1234L) {
  set.seed(seed)
  n  <- nrow(X); TT <- ncol(X)
  w0 <- 1 / lengths(nb_self)
  cards <- lengths(nb_self) - 1L
  self_in <- vapply(seq_len(n), function(i) i %in% nb_self[[i]], logical(1))
  stopifnot(all(self_in))
  p_fold <- matrix(NA_real_, n, TT)
  for (t in seq_len(TT)) {
    sl <- max(1L, t - k):t
    S  <- rowSums(X[, sl, drop = FALSE])
    for (i in seq_len(n)) {
      obs <- sum(S[nb_self[[i]]])
      ci  <- cards[i]
      r   <- replicate(nsim, sample.int(n - 1L, ci))
      r   <- matrix(r, nrow = ci)
      idx <- r + (r >= i)                      # skip the township itself
      sim <- S[i] + colSums(matrix(S[idx], nrow = ci))
      l <- (sum(obs >= sim) + 1) / (nsim + 1)
      g <- (sum(obs <= sim) + 1) / (nsim + 1)
      p_fold[i, t] <- min(l, g)
    }
  }
  # pmin() takes its attributes from its first argument, so the matrix is
  # filled in place rather than rebuilt; otherwise the dimensions are lost.
  p_two <- p_fold
  p_two[] <- pmin(1, 2 * p_fold)
  list(p_fold = p_fold, p_two = p_two)
}

# The class rules. sfdep's own list is used, evaluated in sfdep's order, with one
# correction. In sfdep 0.2.5 the "intensifying hotspot" rule counts significant
# quarters of EITHER sign and never checks that the last one is hot, and it is
# evaluated before "diminishing coldspot". A township that is a significant cold
# spot in 90% of quarters and whose Gi* is rising therefore comes out as an
# intensifying HOT spot. The corrected rule counts only significant hot quarters
# and requires the last one to be hot, which is how sfdep already writes the
# cold version and how Esri defines the class.
ehsa_rules <- function(corrected = TRUE) {
  fx <- sfdep:::fxs
  if (corrected) {
    fx[["intensifying hotspot"]] <- function(gs, sigs, n, tau, tau_p, threshold, ...) {
      (sum(sigs & gs > 0) / n >= 0.9) && sigs[n] && gs[n] > 0 &&
        (tau > 0) && (tau_p < threshold)
    }
  }
  fx
}

# Mann-Kendall on each township's Gi* series, then the class rules. With
# corrected = FALSE this reproduces sfdep:::classify_hotspot() exactly, which is
# checked in scripts/04_ehsa.R, so a difference in the result can come only from
# the p-values fed in or from the one rule that is corrected.
# sfdep spells "oscilating" with one l; it is corrected here, once, for display.
ehsa_classify <- function(G, P, threshold = 0.05, locs, corrected = TRUE) {
  fx <- ehsa_rules(corrected)
  out <- lapply(seq_len(nrow(G)), function(i) {
    gs <- G[i, ]; sigs <- P[i, ] <= threshold; n <- length(gs)
    mk <- Kendall::MannKendall(gs)
    tau <- unname(mk$tau); tau_p <- as.numeric(mk$sl)
    hit <- vapply(fx, function(f) isTRUE(f(gs = gs, sigs = sigs, n = n, tau = tau,
                                            tau_p = tau_p, threshold = threshold)),
                  logical(1))
    data.frame(location = locs[i], tau = tau, p_value = tau_p,
               classification = names(fx)[hit][1])
  })
  res <- do.call(rbind, out)
  res$classification <- sub("oscilating", "oscillating", res$classification)
  res
}

# Esri-style display labels, in the order used by PAL_EHSA in R/utils.R.
ehsa_label <- function(x) {
  x <- sub("hotspot$", "hot spot", sub("coldspot$", "cold spot", x))
  x <- paste0(toupper(substr(x, 1, 1)), substr(x, 2, nchar(x)))
  factor(x, levels = names(PAL_EHSA))
}

# Panel (long, ordered by period then location) to an n_locs x n_times matrix.
panel_matrix <- function(panel, var, locs) {
  periods <- sort(unique(panel$period))
  M <- matrix(NA_real_, length(locs), length(periods),
              dimnames = list(locs, as.character(periods)))
  M[cbind(match(panel$TS_PCODE, locs), match(panel$period, periods))] <- panel[[var]]
  stopifnot(!anyNA(M))
  M
}

# =============================================================================
# R/utils.R  -- shared helpers for the technical report and the analysis scripts
# Take-home Exercise 2 | ISSS626
#
# One typographic and colour system for every graphic in the report, plus the
# caching layer that keeps the permutation-based statistics reproducible
# without recomputing them on every render.
# =============================================================================

suppressPackageStartupMessages({
  library(dplyr); library(ggplot2)
})

# ---- Reproducible caching ---------------------------------------------------
# The conditional permutation tests behind local Moran's I, local Geary's C and
# Gi* are the expensive part of this analysis, and the space-time cube runs
# them once per period. `cache_rds()` evaluates an expression once, stores the
# result, and returns the stored object on later renders. The code that
# produced it stays visible in the report, so caching removes recomputation and
# not transparency. Deleting data/cache/ forces a full recomputation; every
# script sets the same seed, so the recomputed values are identical.
CACHE_DIR <- "data/cache"
dir.create(CACHE_DIR, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

cache_rds <- function(name, expr, refresh = getOption("th2.refresh", FALSE)) {
  f <- file.path(CACHE_DIR, paste0(name, ".rds"))
  if (file.exists(f) && !refresh) return(readRDS(f))
  t0  <- Sys.time()
  val <- force(expr)
  saveRDS(val, f)
  message(sprintf("[cache] computed %-30s %.1fs", name,
                  as.numeric(difftime(Sys.time(), t0, units = "secs"))))
  val
}

`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a

# ---- Colour ------------------------------------------------------------------
# Three palettes, each tied to one statistic, so that a colour means the same
# thing everywhere in the report.
PAL <- list(
  conflict = "#9f1239", conflict_l = "#fb7185", conflict_xl = "#ffe4e6",
  cool     = "#1d4ed8", cool_l     = "#93c5fd",
  grey     = "#57534e", grey_l     = "#d6d3d1", grid = "#e7e5e4",
  ink      = "#1c1917", paper      = "#fcfcfb"
)

# Sequential ramp for counts and rates. Every intensity surface in the report
# uses it, so two choropleths are comparable at a glance.
RAMP_SEQ <- c("#fff7f3", "#fde0dd", "#fcc5c0", "#fa9fb5",
              "#f768a1", "#dd3497", "#ae017e", "#7a0177")

# LISA quadrants. High-High and Low-Low carry the saturated hues because they
# are the clusters; the two spatial-outlier quadrants are deliberately paler so
# that a reader does not confuse an outlier with a cluster.
PAL_LISA <- c(
  "High-High"     = "#b2182b",
  "Low-Low"       = "#2166ac",
  "High-Low"      = "#ef8a62",
  "Low-High"      = "#67a9cf",
  "Insignificant" = "#f0efee"
)

# Gi* hot and cold spots, diverging around zero.
PAL_GI <- c(
  "Hot spot"      = "#b2182b",
  "Cold spot"     = "#2166ac",
  "Insignificant" = "#f0efee"
)

# The eight emerging hot spot categories, in Esri's own ordering so that a
# reader who knows the tool recognises the legend. Hot categories run warm,
# cold categories run cool, and anything the test cannot classify stays grey.
PAL_EHSA <- c(
  "New hot spot"           = "#fcae91",
  "Consecutive hot spot"   = "#fb6a4a",
  "Intensifying hot spot"  = "#de2d26",
  "Persistent hot spot"    = "#a50f15",
  "Diminishing hot spot"   = "#fdd0a2",
  "Sporadic hot spot"      = "#fdae6b",
  "Oscillating hot spot"   = "#e6550d",
  "Historical hot spot"    = "#8c2d04",
  "New cold spot"          = "#c6dbef",
  "Consecutive cold spot"  = "#6baed6",
  "Intensifying cold spot" = "#2171b5",
  "Persistent cold spot"   = "#08306b",
  "Diminishing cold spot"  = "#dadaeb",
  "Sporadic cold spot"     = "#9e9ac8",
  "Oscillating cold spot"  = "#6a51a3",
  "Historical cold spot"   = "#3f007d",
  "No pattern detected"    = "#f0efee"
)

# ---- Presentation -----------------------------------------------------------
theme_th <- function(base_size = 12) {
  theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      plot.title       = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.05),
                                      margin = margin(b = 2)),
      plot.subtitle    = element_text(colour = PAL$grey, size = rel(0.88),
                                      margin = margin(b = 9)),
      plot.caption     = element_text(colour = PAL$grey, size = rel(0.74),
                                      hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 9)),
      axis.title       = element_text(size = rel(0.86)),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.28, colour = PAL$grid),
      strip.text       = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(0.85)),
      legend.position  = "bottom",
      legend.key.height = unit(0.4, "cm"),
      legend.title     = element_text(size = rel(0.82)),
      legend.text      = element_text(size = rel(0.78)),
      plot.title.position   = "plot",
      plot.caption.position = "plot"
    )
}

theme_map <- function(base_size = 11) {
  theme_th(base_size) +
    theme(
      axis.text        = element_blank(),
      axis.title       = element_blank(),
      axis.ticks       = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major = element_line(linewidth = 0.2, colour = "#f0efee"),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = PAL$paper, colour = NA),
      panel.border     = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = PAL$grid,
                                      linewidth = 0.4),
      legend.position  = "right",
      legend.key.width = unit(0.32, "cm"),
      legend.key.height = unit(1.0, "cm")
    )
}

# ---- Formatters --------------------------------------------------------------
n_fmt <- function(x, d = 0) formatC(x, format = "f", big.mark = ",", digits = d)

pct <- function(x, d = 1) paste0(formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d), "%")

# Vectorised: several tables format a whole column of p-values at once.
pv <- function(p) {
  vapply(p, function(x) {
    if (is.na(x)) return("NA")
    if (x < 0.001) return("< 0.001")
    formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 3)
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}

# Kendall's tau carries a sign that matters, so it is never shown unsigned.
tau_fmt <- function(x, d = 3) {
  sprintf("%s%s", ifelse(x >= 0, "+", "−"),
          formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = d))
}

# ---- Significance ------------------------------------------------------------
# Every local statistic in this report is tested at each of 330 townships at
# once. Reporting the raw 0.05 threshold alone would put roughly 17 false
# positives on each map, so both the raw and the false-discovery-rate adjusted
# verdicts are carried through and the maps say which one they are drawing.
sig_flag <- function(p, alpha = 0.05, method = c("none", "fdr", "bonferroni")) {
  method <- match.arg(method)
  if (method == "none") return(p < alpha)
  p.adjust(p, method = method) < alpha
}

# Expected number of false positives at a given threshold, used in the prose so
# that a count of significant townships is never quoted without its benchmark.
expected_fp <- function(n, alpha = 0.05) n * alpha

# ---- LISA classification -----------------------------------------------------
# The quadrant label is built from the sign of the centred value and the sign of
# its centred spatial lag, not from any quadrant field a package happens to
# return: that keeps the label meaning the same regardless of which
# implementation produced the statistic.
lisa_quadrant <- function(x, lag_x, p, alpha = 0.05,
                          method = c("none", "fdr", "bonferroni")) {
  sig <- sig_flag(p, alpha, match.arg(method))
  xc  <- x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  lc  <- lag_x - mean(lag_x, na.rm = TRUE)
  out <- ifelse(xc > 0 & lc > 0, "High-High",
         ifelse(xc < 0 & lc < 0, "Low-Low",
         ifelse(xc > 0 & lc < 0, "High-Low", "Low-High")))
  out[!sig | is.na(sig)] <- "Insignificant"
  factor(out, levels = names(PAL_LISA))
}

# Hot and cold spots are read off the SIGN OF Gi*, which is what the statistic
# measures: whether the neighbourhood sum around a township is large or small
# relative to the whole study area.
gi_class <- function(gi_star, p, alpha = 0.05,
                     method = c("none", "fdr", "bonferroni")) {
  sig <- sig_flag(p, alpha, match.arg(method))
  out <- ifelse(gi_star > 0, "Hot spot", "Cold spot")
  out[!sig | is.na(sig)] <- "Insignificant"
  factor(out, levels = names(PAL_GI))
}

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Fire on Drained Peat课后作业一：排水泥炭地上的火
text:
Abstract摘要

Pulang Pisau Regency holds much of the drainage network left behind by Indonesia’s abandoned Mega Rice Project, and it burns in almost every dry season. This report treats 3,101 VIIRS 375 m active-fire detections, recorded inside the regency between 4 and 11 September 2026, as one realisation of a spatial and spatio-temporal point process.
Detection intensity varies about fortyfold across the regency. It rises sharply close to engineered canals and falls close to natural rivers. The two effects keep opposite signs after multivariate adjustment, and that is what separates a drainage mechanism from simple proximity to water.
The second-order analysis is built around a sequence of null models, and its main result is methodological. A homogeneous Poisson null is rejected, but the rejection carries no information. A kernel-based inhomogeneous Poisson null then gives opposite answers at different intensity bandwidths. It is not rejected at 1–2 km. At 10 km it is rejected decisively. We read this as a problem of identifiability and statistical power, not as a finding about fire. The p-value falls monotonically as the null becomes less flexible, so the verdict is tracking the model and not the data. Replacing the kernel with a parsimonious parametric null breaks the impasse. A covariate-driven Poisson process is rejected. A Thomas cluster process carrying the same trend is not, and it estimates compact clusters of roughly 2.1 km.
A Monte-Carlo Knox test on permuted dates then establishes genuine space-time interaction, using no bandwidth and no covariates at all. Throughout, the analysis keeps the behaviour of the fire field separate from the behaviour of the satellite. That distinction accounts for most of the apparent day-to-day variation.


Pulang Pisau 县境内保留着印尼「百万公顷稻米工程」遗留的大片排水渠网,几乎每个 旱季都会过火。本报告把 2026 年 9 月 4 日至 11 日该县记录到的 3,101 个 VIIRS 375 m 活跃火点探测,视为一次空间与时空点过程的实现加以分析。
一阶分析显示,探测强度在全县范围内相差约四十倍。它在人工运河附近明显升高, 在天然河流附近反而降低。两者的方向在多变量调整之后依然相反,正是这一点把 排水机制与泛泛的「靠水」区分开来。
二阶分析围绕一组逐层放宽的零模型展开,其主要结果属于方法学层面。齐次泊松 零模型被拒绝,但这一拒绝不提供任何信息。改用基于核的非齐次泊松零模型之后,不同的 强度带宽给出了相反的答案:在 1–2 km 下不被拒绝,在 10 km 下被决定性地拒绝。 我们把它判断为可识别性与检验力的问题,而不是关于火本身的发现。随着零模型变得 不那么灵活,p 值单调下降,说明判定追踪的是模型而不是数据。把核估计换成一个简约的 参数化零模型可以打破僵局。由协变量驱动的泊松过程被拒绝;带有同一趋势项的 Thomas 聚集过程没有被拒绝,并估计出约 2.1 km 的紧凑簇群。
随后,在置换日期上进行的蒙特卡洛 Knox 检验确立了真实的时空交互,整个过程既不使用 带宽,也不使用任何协变量。全篇始终把火场的行为与卫星的行为分开来看。这一区分 解释了逐日表观变化中的大部分。

section: 1.1 Why peatland fire is a public-safety problem泥炭地火灾为何是公共安全问题
text:
1.1 Why peatland fire is a public-safety problem泥炭地火灾为何是公共安全问题

Public safety in the Indonesian peatland provinces is shaped every dry season by fire. The hazard is not primarily flame. Peat burns below ground, slowly, over weeks, and its dominant health impact is transboundary smoke: the 1997 Indonesian peat and forest fires released on the order of 0.81–2.57 Gt of carbon, an amount comparable to a substantial fraction of annual global fossil fuel emissions at the time (Page et al., 2002), and Indonesian fire activity has been shown to respond non-linearly to El Niño-induced drought, so that moderate increases in dryness produce disproportionate increases in smoke pollution (Field et al., 2016). The exposed population is large, the exposure pathway is respiratory, and the events that generate it are spatially discrete ignitions that can, in principle, be anticipated and prevented.
Pulang Pisau Regency, in Central Kalimantan, is a particularly consequential place to study this. Between 1995 and 1999 the Indonesian government’s Mega Rice Project (Proyek Lahan Gambut Sejuta Hektar) attempted to convert approximately one million hectares of peat swamp forest in Central Kalimantan to rice cultivation. Several thousand kilometres of drainage canals were excavated before the project was terminated by Presidential Decree 80/1999 (Ritzema et al., 2014). The canals remain. They lower the peat water table, the dried peat becomes combustible, and the area has burned repeatedly since (Hoscilo et al., 2011; Konecny et al., 2016). Ignition itself is overwhelmingly human: Cattau et al. (2016) attribute the great majority of ignitions on this landscape to land preparation and related activity rather than natural causes.
That combination (an engineered hydrological cause, a human ignition source, and a recurring seasonal hazard) makes the location and timing of fire events the natural object of analysis, and makes point pattern analysis the natural method.


印尼泥炭地各省的公共安全,每年旱季都由火灾主导。真正的危害主要不是明火。泥炭在地下缓慢燃烧,可持续数周,其主要健康影响是跨境烟霾:1997 年印尼泥炭与森林大火释放了约 0.81–2.57 Gt 碳,相当于当时全球年度化石燃料排放量的可观比例 (Page et al., 2002);研究还表明印尼火灾活动对厄尔尼诺引发的干旱呈非线性响应,即干燥程度的中等增加会带来烟霾污染的不成比例上升 (Field et al., 2016)。暴露人口规模大,暴露途径是呼吸道,而产生烟霾的事件是空间上离散的点火行为,原则上可以预判、也可以预防。
中加里曼丹的 Pulang Pisau 县是研究这一问题特别有意义的地点。1995 至 1999 年间,印尼政府的”百万公顷稻米工程”(Proyek Lahan Gambut Sejuta Hektar)试图将中加里曼丹约一百万公顷泥炭沼泽林改造为稻田。在工程被第 80/1999 号总统令终止之前,已开挖了数千公里排水运河 (Ritzema et al., 2014)。这些运河至今仍在。它们压低泥炭地下水位,干化的泥炭变得可燃,此后该地区反复过火 (Hoscilo et al., 2011; Konecny et al., 2016)。点火源则绝大多数来自人为:Cattau 等人 (2016) 将该景观上的绝大部分点火归因于土地整备及相关活动,而非自然原因。
这三者的组合(一个工程性的水文成因、一个人为点火源、以及一个反复出现的季节性灾害)使火灾事件的位置与时间成为自然的分析对象,也使点模式分析成为自然的方法。

section: 1.2 Why point pattern analysis, and what it can and cannot say为什么用点模式分析,以及它能说与不能说什么
text:
1.2 Why point pattern analysis, and what it can and cannot say为什么用点模式分析,以及它能说与不能说什么

A set of satellite fire detections is a point pattern: a finite set of locations, in a bounded window, generated by a process we do not observe directly. Point pattern analysis distinguishes two properties of that process, and the distinction organises this entire report.


一组卫星火点探测就是一个点模式:在有界窗口内的有限位置集合,由一个我们无法直接观测的过程生成。点模式分析区分该过程的两种性质,而这一区分贯穿整份报告的组织结构。








NoteFirst-order and second-order properties



First-order properties concern the intensity function \(\lambda(u)\), the expected number of events per unit area at location \(u\). First-order analysis asks where are events more or less likely, and treats each location’s propensity as a property of the location.
Second-order properties concern interaction between events, whether the presence of an event at \(u\) changes the probability of an event near \(u\), over and above whatever \(\lambda(u)\) already implies. Second-order analysis asks do events attract, repel, or ignore one another.
The two are fundamentally confounded in a single realisation (A. Baddeley et al., 2015, ch. 7). A pattern with many points in one corner can be described either as high intensity there (first-order) or as clustering (second-order), and no amount of data from one realisation can separate them without an assumption. This report therefore does not pretend to separate them by choosing a better statistic; it separates them by stating an explicit assumption about the scale at which each operates, and then testing how much the conclusions depend on that assumption.










Note一阶性质与二阶性质



一阶性质关注强度函数 \(\lambda(u)\),位置 \(u\) 处单位面积的期望事件数。一阶分析问的是事件在哪里更容易发生、哪里更不容易,并把每个位置的倾向视为该位置本身的属性。
二阶性质关注事件之间的交互,\(u\) 处存在一个事件,是否会在 \(\lambda(u)\) 已隐含的程度之外,改变 \(u\) 附近出现事件的概率。二阶分析问的是事件之间相互吸引、相互排斥,还是彼此无关。
在单次实现中,这两者从根本上是混淆的 (A. Baddeley et al., 2015, ch. 7)。某个角落点很多的模式,既可以描述为那里强度高(一阶),也可以描述为聚集(二阶);仅凭一次实现的数据,无论多少,都无法在不引入假设的情况下把两者分开。因此这里并不假装靠挑一个更好的统计量来分离它们;而是通过明确陈述关于两者各自作用尺度的假设来分离,然后检验结论在多大程度上依赖该假设。




Equally important is what the data are. A FIRMS record is not a fire. It is a detection: a satellite pixel that a thermal anomaly algorithm flagged during one overpass (Schroeder et al., 2014). One fire can produce many detections; one fire can produce none, if it burns under cloud or between overpasses. Any pattern in the detections is therefore a pattern in
\[
\text{fire activity} \;\times\; \text{observation process},
\]
and separating these two is a data-quality problem before it is a statistical one. Section 4 returns to this, and Section 5.1 shows that in this dataset the observation process accounts for a large part of the apparent day-to-day variation.


同样重要的是数据究竟是什么。一条 FIRMS 记录不是一场火。它是一次探测:某次卫星过境时,热异常算法标记出来的一个像元 (Schroeder et al., 2014)。一场火可以产生许多条探测;一场火也可能一条都不产生,如果它在云层下燃烧,或在两次过境之间烧完。因此探测点中的任何模式,实际上是
\[
\text{火灾活动} \;\times\; \text{观测过程}
\]
的模式,而分离这两者首先是一个数据质量问题,其次才是统计问题。4 节会回到这一点,5.1 节则表明:在本数据集中,观测过程解释了逐日变化中的很大一部分。

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Fire on Drained Peat课后作业一：排水泥炭地上的火
text:
1.3 Research questions研究问题

The analysis is organised around six questions, three first-order and three second-order.


分析围绕六个问题展开,三个属于一阶,三个属于二阶。



RQ1 (first-order, space. How does the intensity of active-fire detection vary across Pulang Pisau Regency, and at what spatial scale can that variation legitimately be resolved given a 375 m sensor?


RQ2) first-order, time. Does detection intensity vary from day to day within the observation window, and can genuine variation in fire activity be distinguished from variation in satellite sampling?


RQ3 (first-order, covariates. Is detection intensity associated with proximity to the engineered drainage network, as distinct from proximity to natural rivers, roads, or settlements?


RQ4) second-order, space. After the large-scale intensity gradient is accounted for, do detections show evidence of clustering, inhibition, or approximate randomness (and over what range of distances?


RQ5) second-order, space-time. Is there space-time interaction: are detections that are close in space also close in time, beyond what their separate spatial and temporal patterns imply?


RQ6 (value added. Can measured drainage and access geography account for the observed clustering, or does excess clustering remain once that geography is modelled) and what generative process best describes it?




RQ1 (一阶,空间。 活跃火点探测强度在 Pulang Pisau 县内如何变化?在 375 m 分辨率传感器的前提下,这种变化在什么空间尺度上才是可以正当分辨的?


RQ2) 一阶,时间。 在观测窗口内,探测强度是否逐日变化?火灾活动的真实变化能否与卫星采样的变化区分开?


RQ3 (一阶,协变量。 探测强度是否与到人工排水网络的邻近度相关?这一关联能否与到天然河流、道路或居民点的邻近度区分开?


RQ4) 二阶,空间。 在扣除大尺度强度梯度之后,探测点是否表现出聚集、抑制或近似随机的证据?在什么距离范围内?


RQ5 (二阶,时空。 是否存在时空交互:空间上靠近的探测点在时间上是否也靠近,其程度是否超出各自的空间格局与时间格局所隐含的水平?


RQ6) 增值分析。 已测得的排水与可达性地理条件能否解释观测到的聚集?在对该地理条件建模之后是否仍有超额聚集?什么样的生成过程能最好地描述它?

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Fire on Drained Peat课后作业一：排水泥炭地上的火
text:
1.4 Objectives研究目标


Prepare and integrate satellite fire-detection data, official administrative boundaries and contextual infrastructure data into a defensible point pattern, with a complete and auditable record of every data-quality decision.
Characterise first-order properties in space, in time, and as a function of covariates.
Characterise second-order properties against explicitly justified null models rather than against a default one.
State and evaluate the assumptions each method requires, and quantify how far the conclusions depend on them.
Communicate the findings through geovisualisations and statistical graphics designed for analytical reading.
Translate the evidence into implications for public-safety planning, while separating what the analysis supports from what it does not.




将卫星火点探测数据、官方行政边界与背景基础设施数据准备并整合为一个站得住脚的点模式,并对每一项数据质量决策留下完整可审计的记录。
刻画空间上、时间上以及作为协变量函数的一阶性质。
针对有明确论证的零模型(而非默认零模型)刻画二阶性质。
陈述并评估每种方法所需的假设,并量化结论对这些假设的依赖程度。
通过为分析性阅读而设计的地理可视化与统计图形传达发现。
将证据转化为对公共安全规划的启示,同时区分分析支持的结论与分析不支持的结论。

Figure 1: Study area. Left: Pulang Pisau Regency within Kalimantan, with all VIIRS S-NPP detections recorded across the island in the same eight days. Right: the regency, its eight kecamatan, and the drainage geography that motivates the analysis.研究区。左:Pulang Pisau 县在加里曼丹岛中的位置,叠加同一八天内全岛的 VIIRS S-NPP 探测点。右:该县、其八个区(kecamatan),以及引出本研究问题的排水地理格局。






Across the island. Kalimantan burned widely in this week (22,763 S-NPP detections island-wide), but activity is patchy, and Pulang Pisau sits inside one of the densest southern clusters. Within the regency, the canal network (thin blue) is dense in the centre and south and sparse in the forested north, while natural rivers (thick blue) run broadly north–south. Settlements are few and align with the rivers and the canal grid. The visual expectation this sets up (that fire should follow the canal grid rather than the rivers) is tested formally in § 5.5 and should not be read off this map, which shows infrastructure, not fire. One limit: OSM completeness is uneven and is likely better near settlements, which could by itself produce an apparent canal–fire association.


放到全岛看。 本周加里曼丹全岛普遍过火(全岛 22,763 个 S-NPP 探测点)但活动呈斑块状,而 Pulang Pisau 正位于南部最密集的簇群之一。县内运河网络(细蓝线)在中部与南部密集、在北部林区 稀疏;天然河流(粗蓝线)大致南北走向。居民点数量不多,沿河流与运河格网分布。 本图建立的视觉预期(火应跟随运河格网而非河流)将在 § 5.5 中 正式检验,不应直接从本图读出结论:本图显示的是基础设施,不是火。 一点限度: OSM 完备性并不均匀,在居民点附近很可能更好,仅此一点就足以造成 「运河, 火」关联的假象。

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Fire on Drained Peat课后作业一：排水泥炭地上的火
section: 2.3 What counts as a point event什么算一个点事件
text:
2.3 What counts as a point event什么算一个点事件

This is the single most consequential definitional decision in the study, and it has no unique right answer.
A FIRMS record is one pixel-overpass: the algorithm flagged a 375 m pixel as containing active fire during one satellite pass (Schroeder et al., 2014). Treating each record as a point event therefore builds three kinds of duplication into the pattern:

Spatial duplication, a single burning area spans several adjacent pixels, all of which are flagged.
Temporal duplication within a day, S-NPP passes roughly twice daily, so a fire burning for a full day can be flagged twice at the same location.
Multi-day persistence, peat fires smoulder for days or weeks, and the same pixel recurs.

Only the third of these is a property of fire. The first two are properties of the sensor. Because they operate at scales (375 m; 0 m) below the scales at which any substantive question is posed, they would inflate exactly the small-distance clustering that a second-order analysis is designed to detect.
Three analysis units are therefore constructed, and every second-order result is reported for all three.


这是全研究中最具决定性影响的定义性抉择,而且它没有唯一正确的答案。
一条 FIRMS 记录是一次像元-过境:算法在某次卫星过境时把一个 375 m 像元标记为 含有活跃火 (Schroeder et al., 2014)。因此,若把每条记录都当作一个点事件,就会把三种重复 性内建进模式:

空间重复,一片燃烧区域横跨若干相邻像元,这些像元全部被标记。
日内时间重复,S-NPP 每天约过境两次,因此烧了一整天的火可能在同一位置被 标记两次。
跨日持续,泥炭火会阴燃数天甚至数周,同一像元反复出现。

其中只有第三种是火的性质,前两种是传感器的性质。由于它们作用的尺度 (375 m;0 m)低于任何实质性问题所设定的尺度,它们恰恰会放大二阶分析本就要 检测的小距离聚集。
因此构建三种分析单元,且每一项二阶结果都对三者分别报告。



Code
tibble::tibble(
  Unit = c("**Detection**", "**Pixel-day** *(primary)*", "**Event**"),
  Definition = c(
    "Every retained record: one 375 m pixel in one overpass.",
    "One point per unique 375 m grid cell per **local** calendar day; among duplicates the highest-FRP record is kept.",
    "Single-linkage cluster of pixel-days within 750 m *and* 1 day of one another, reduced to its centroid."),
  n = c(N_DET, N_PX, N_EV),
  Removes = c(
    "nothing",
    "same-day repeat overpasses of one pixel",
    "spatial extent and multi-day persistence of one burning area"),
  Interprets_as = c(
    "detection intensity, closest to the raw observation",
    "daily fire-affected pixel, the compromise used throughout",
    "approximate distinct fire event, i.e. nearest to *ignitions*")
) |>
  gt::gt() |>
  gt::cols_label(Interprets_as = "Interpreted as") |>
  gt::fmt_markdown(columns = c(Unit)) |>
  gt::fmt_number(columns = n, decimals = 0) |>
  gt::tab_options(table.font.size = gt::pct(84),
                  data_row.padding = gt::px(6))

Table 2: The three analysis units. The pixel-day unit is used for all headline results.三种分析单元。所有主要结果均采用「像元-日」单元。





The pixel-day unit is primary because it removes the duplication that is purely instrumental (repeat overpasses) without discarding the duplication that is substantively meaningful (a pixel that burns on several successive days is genuinely burning on several successive days). The event unit is the most appealing conceptually, but § 6.5 shows that at this fire density single-linkage chaining merges much of the landscape into one component, so it is used for robustness rather than for headline results.


之所以以「像元-日」为主单元,是因为它剔除了纯属仪器性的重复(重复过境),同时 保留了实质上有意义的重复(某像元连续几天燃烧,就是真的连续几天在烧)。「事件」 单元在概念上最有吸引力,但 § 6.5 表明:在本例的火密度下,单连接 链式合并会把大片景观并成一个连通分量,因此该单元仅用于稳健性检验,而非主要结果。

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Fire on Drained Peat课后作业一：排水泥炭地上的火
section: 2.4 Spatial study window空间研究窗口
text:
2.4 Spatial study window空间研究窗口

The window is Pulang Pisau Regency as delineated in the official COD-AB ADM2 layer (Badan Pusat Statistik & United Nations OCHA Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, 2026), projected to EPSG:32749.


研究窗口为官方 COD-AB ADM2 图层 (Badan Pusat Statistik & United Nations OCHA Regional Office for Asia and the Pacific, 2026) 界定的 Pulang Pisau 县, 投影至 EPSG:32749。


Three choices need defending.
Why an administrative boundary at all? A point process must be analysed inside a window that is defined independently of the points; otherwise edge effects and intensity estimates are conditioned on the data. Candidate windows were a regency boundary, a peat-hydrological unit, and a convex or concave hull of the detections. The hull is disqualified outright. It is defined by the data. A hydrological unit would be scientifically preferable, since the process is hydrological, but it does not correspond to any administrative mandate. The regency is chosen because it is the unit that owns the response: fire suppression, land-use permitting and village-level prevention budgets are administered at regency and kecamatan level, so findings expressed on this window are directly actionable. The cost is that the boundary is arbitrary with respect to the fire process, and § 6.5 tests the consequence.


有三项选择需要论证。
为什么要用行政边界? 点过程必须在一个独立于点本身定义的窗口内分析,否则 边界效应与强度估计都会被数据所条件化。候选窗口有三种:县界、泥炭水文单元,以及 探测点的凸包/凹包。凸包直接被排除。它是由数据定义的。水文单元在科学上更可取 (该过程本身就是水文性的),但它不对应任何行政职责。最终选择县界,因为它是 承担应对责任的单元:灭火、土地利用许可与村级预防预算都在县与区(kecamatan) 层级管理,因此在这一窗口上表述的发现可以直接落地。代价是该边界相对于火灾过程是 任意的,§ 6.5 检验了这一代价的后果。


Why the official COD-AB layer? It is sourced from Badan Pusat Statistik and carries a stated validity date (boundaries valid from 1 April 2020), a version, and kecamatan-level nesting. The independently produced geoBoundaries ADM2 polygon for the same regency gives an area of 9758.9 km² against 9758.9 km² here (a difference of 0.00%), which is reassuring, and unsurprising, since both ultimately derive from the same BPS geometry.
What is the window’s actual extent? The polygon is a single part, topologically valid, with 4,179 vertices. Its area is 9,759 km², closely matching the area_sqkm attribute carried in the source file (9741 km²). It is strongly elongated: 86 km east–west by 213 km north–south. This matters twice over: it caps the distance at which second-order functions can be estimated (§ 6.1), and it makes a single isotropic kernel bandwidth a stronger assumption than it would be in a compact window (§ 5.3). The southern boundary is a coast, so part of the perimeter borders water rather than land, a further source of edge effect that no edge correction models, because those corrections assume the process continues beyond the boundary.


为什么用官方 COD-AB 图层? 它源自印尼中央统计局(Badan Pusat Statistik), 带有明确生效日期(边界自 2020 年 4 月 1 日起有效)、版本号,以及区级嵌套结构。 独立制作的 geoBoundaries ADM2 多边形对同一个县给出面积 9758.9 km²,本研究为 9758.9 km², 差异 0.00%。这既令人放心 也不意外,因为两者最终都源自同一套 BPS 几何。
这个窗口的实际范围是什么? 该多边形为单一部件、拓扑有效,共 4,179 个顶点。面积 9,759 km²,与源文件所带 area_sqkm 属性 (9741 km²)高度一致。其形状高度狭长:东西向 86 km,南北向 213 km。这有双重影响:它限制了二阶函数 可被估计的最大距离(§ 6.1),也使「单一各向同性核带宽」这一假设比在 紧凑窗口中更强(§ 5.3)。南界为海岸线,因此部分周长临水而非临陆 。这是又一处边界效应来源,而任何边界校正都无法建模它,因为那些校正都假定过程在 边界之外继续存在。

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Fire on Drained Peat课后作业一：排水泥炭地上的火
section: 2.5 Temporal study window时间研究窗口
text:
2.5 Temporal study window时间研究窗口

The analysis covers 04 September to 11 September 2026 (8 local days), which is the full extent of the open FIRMS archive at the time of access.
This is a short window, and honesty about what it can support matters more than apparent sophistication:

It falls in the peak of the Central Kalimantan dry season, so it captures the hazard at its most intense, not as an annual average. Conclusions describe a burning episode, not a fire year.
No seasonality can be estimated. Questions about monthly or inter-annual variation are outside the reach of these data, and are not asked.
Temporal aggregation is to the local calendar day. Finer aggregation is impossible: as § 5.1 shows, S-NPP contributes detections at only about two local times per day, so anything finer than a day would describe the satellite’s orbit rather than the fire’s behaviour.
Eight days is enough for a space-time interaction test at lags of 0–5 days (§ 6.6), which is the relevant scale for fire spread and for day-to-day ignition decisions, but not for anything longer.

The authenticated acquisition script is included precisely so that this limitation is removable: supplying a FIRMS MAP_KEY and rerunning scripts/01_download_firms.R with a wider date range reproduces every result below over a full season, with no change to any other file.


分析覆盖 2026-09-04 至 2026-09-11,共 8 个当地日,即访问时开放 FIRMS 档案的全部范围。
这是一个很短的窗口,而诚实说明它能支持什么,比表面上的复杂度更重要:

它正落在中加里曼丹旱季峰值,因此捕捉到的是灾害最强烈的状态,而非年度平均。 结论描述的是一次燃烧事件,不是一个火年。
无法估计季节性。 月际或年际变化的问题超出本数据能力范围,故本报告不提出。
时间聚合到当地日历日。更细的聚合不可能:如 § 5.1 所示,S-NPP 每天只在约两个当地时刻贡献探测,因此任何比「日」更细的粒度描述的都是卫星轨道, 而不是火的行为。
八天足以支持滞后 0–5 天的时空交互检验(§ 6.6),这正是火蔓延与逐日点火 决策的相关尺度;但不足以支持更长尺度的分析。

之所以把需认证的获取脚本一并纳入,正是为了让这一局限可以被移除:提供 FIRMS MAP_KEY 并以更宽日期范围重跑 scripts/01_download_firms.R,即可在整个火季上 复现下文全部结果,其余文件一行都不需要改。

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Fire on Drained Peat课后作业一：排水泥炭地上的火
section: 3.1 Import and schema harmonisation数据导入与模式统一
text:
3.1 Import and schema harmonisation数据导入与模式统一

Every column is read as character first. This is deliberate: if readr guessed a numeric type it would coerce a malformed coordinate to NA during parsing, and the record would be lost before it could be counted as a data fault. Numeric coercion happens afterwards, under our own control.
The four products do not share a schema. VIIRS reports channel brightness temperatures as bright_ti4 (4 µm) and bright_ti5 (11 µm); MODIS reports brightness and bright_t31. Confidence is a three-level ordinal class for VIIRS (low/nominal/high), but an integer percentage 0–100 for MODIS. These are mapped onto common fields (bt_fire, bt_bg, confidence_cls), so that one filtering rule can be stated, while firms_source preserves the provenance of every row.


所有列先一律按 character 读入。这是刻意的:如果让 readr 猜测数值类型,它会在 解析阶段就把格式错误的坐标强制转成 NA,该记录在能被计为一个数据缺陷之前就已经 丢失了。数值转换在此之后、由我们自己控制地进行。
四种产品的数据模式并不一致。VIIRS 用 bright_ti4(4 µm)和 bright_ti5(11 µm) 报告通道亮温;MODIS 用 brightness 和 bright_t31。置信度在 VIIRS 中是三级有序 分类(low/nominal/high),在 MODIS 中却是 0–100 的整数百分比。这些字段被 映射到统一字段(bt_fire、bt_bg、confidence_cls),以便用一条筛选规则表述; 同时 firms_source 保留每一行的来源出处。



Confidence harmonisation rule
fires |> mutate(confidence_cls = case_when(
  sensor_family == "VIIRS" & str_starts(str_to_lower(confidence_raw), "l") ~ "low",
  sensor_family == "VIIRS" & str_starts(str_to_lower(confidence_raw), "n") ~ "nominal",
  sensor_family == "VIIRS" & str_starts(str_to_lower(confidence_raw), "h") ~ "high",
  sensor_family == "MODIS" & conf_num <  30 ~ "low",      # MODIS 0-100 scale
  sensor_family == "MODIS" & conf_num <  80 ~ "nominal",
  sensor_family == "MODIS" & conf_num >= 80 ~ "high"))

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Fire on Drained Peat课后作业一：排水泥炭地上的火
section: 3.2 Coordinates: validity, and a precision trap坐标:有效性,以及一个精度陷阱
text:
3.2 Coordinates: validity, and a precision trap坐标:有效性,以及一个精度陷阱

No record had a missing or non-numeric coordinate, and none fell outside valid geographic ranges or on the (0, 0) null island, checks that cost nothing and would have been serious if they had fired.
There is, however, a subtler issue. Latitudes are written with between one and five decimal places:


没有任何记录出现坐标缺失或非数值的情况,也没有任何记录落在有效地理范围之外或 (0, 0) 这个「空岛」上。这些检查成本为零,但一旦触发就会很严重。
不过存在一个更微妙的问题。纬度的小数位数在一位到五位之间不等:



Code
raw_chk <- readr::read_csv(
  list.files("data/raw", "^firms_pulangpisau_.*[.]csv$", full.names = TRUE)[1],
  show_col_types = FALSE, col_types = readr::cols(.default = readr::col_character()))
tibble(dp = nchar(stringr::str_replace(raw_chk$latitude, "^[^.]*[.]?", ""))) |>
  count(dp, name = "records") |>
  mutate(`implied precision` = scales::label_comma(accuracy = 0.01)(111320 / 10^dp),
         `implied precision` = paste0(`implied precision`, " m")) |>
  gt::gt() |> gt::cols_label(dp = "Decimal places") |>
  gt::tab_options(table.font.size = gt::pct(85), data_row.padding = gt::px(4))
